it simply checks packets against a rule table without considering the state of the connection. For instance, an administrator can configure the firewall to block traffic on specific ports, such as preventing a workstation from using port 25 to avoid spreading email viruses.

operates reactively rather than proactively. It analyzes packets in motion, inspects patterns, and flags anomalies, allowing security teams to investigate and respond to potential incidents. This passive monitoring approach is advantageous for detecting subtle or sophisticated threats, such as zero-day exploits or insider attacks, that may bypass traditional preventive mechanisms. However, its limitation lies in the fact that it does not actively protect the network or endpoints, leaving the system vulnerable until human intervention occur

By contrast, a firewall functions as a proactive gatekeeper. It actively monitors traffic
and enforces security policies to prevent threats from escalating into incidents.

which only signals potential threats, firewalls are capable of intervening in real time,

In contrast with a classical firewall which refers to the traditional configuration model in which firewall policy is applied on interfaces

a configuration model in which interfaces are assigned to security zones, and firewall policy is applied to traffic moving between the zones. If an additional interface is added to the private zone, the hosts connected to the new interface in the private zone can pass traffic to all hosts on the existing interface in the same zone

the network is segmented into zones based on trust and functionality, traffic flows between zones are explicitly defined using zone pairs, and class maps and policy maps are used to match and control specific types of traffic. By default, all traffic is denied unless explicitly permitted, ensuring a least-privilege, default-deny security posture. Policies can include inspection, logging, and specific permissions, while monitoring and testing ensure proper enforcement.
